253.title: Kabir the weaver
253.hook: Kabir of Benares, a weaver, sang in plain speech that no priest or custom stood between the soul and God
253.howItsDone: Kabir's hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Sikh kirtan alongside the Gurus' own, in the same ragas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhagat: truth has many singers. Today, the first of two Bhagats this path stays with for a while.

Benares, on the Ganges: temples, priests, pilgrims, scholars arguing in Sanskrit. And in a narrow lane, the clack of a handloom. A weaver sits at it, throwing the shuttle back and forth, singing as he works. Not in Sanskrit. In the plain speech of the street, sharp enough to make a priest wince and a laborer laugh. His name was Kabir, and the Sikh Gurus kept his songs in their book.
screen: `BENARES, THE HOLY CITY.` → `A LOOM IN A LANE.` → `A WEAVER, SINGING.`

segments.voice: Honest start: very little about Kabir's life is certain, and scholars disagree about his dates. In his own verses he calls himself a julaha, a weaver; tradition says he grew up in a Muslim weaving family in Benares and learned from the Hindu teacher Ramanand. Beyond that, much of what's told is legend. His songs are what remain, and the Guru Granth Sahib keeps a great many of them. What did he sing? That nothing stands between the soul and God: not the priest, not the mullah, not birth, not pilgrimage. In a hymn in Rag Gauri he turns on caste pride with a joke: if you're a Brahmin, born of a Brahmin mother, why didn't you come into the world by some other way? Everyone arrives the same way. He was just as blunt about empty ritual in any religion. And the loom? In a hymn in Rag Gujri, his mother weeps: how will these children live? Kabir has given up spinning and weaving and written God's Name on his body. Kabir answers that while threading the shuttle he forgets his Beloved, and that one Provider looks after them all. So he made no neat peace with his trade. But he never stopped thinking like a weaver. In Rag Asa he calls God the weaver whose secret no one knows, who stretched the warp of the whole world, earth and sky for a loom, sun and moon for two shuttles. A weaver's own tools became his picture of God at work. Hence today's line: the loom is the prayer.

segments.voice: Choose one task in front of you today: a job, a class, the dishes, a child's bedtime. Picture doing it the way Kabir sat at the loom, attentive, steady, every motion counted, not rushing to be done. If you pray, let the rhythm of the work carry a word you remember by; if not, let it carry the breath.
Julaha, weaver. Kabir, a weaver of Benares whose plain, sharp songs, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, say nothing stands between the soul and God.
Your line: the loom is the prayer. Even a shuttle can point to God. Day two hundred fifty-three, done.

254.title: Kabir: one light made all
254.hook: first came the light, and all creation from it, so who is good and who is bad (Prabhati, Kabir, ang 1349)
254.howItsDone: Kabir's verse awal allah noor upaaiaa is sung as a shabad in Sikh kirtan and quoted by Sikhs to speak of the oneness of humanity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir the weaver: the loom is the prayer. Today, a verse of his that begins with light.

Light a single candle in a dark room. Light a second from it, a third from that, a hundred more down a long hall. Which flame is the real one? Which is higher-born? It's a silly question. They're all the first flame, passed along. Kabir's Benares had plenty of labels: Hindu and Muslim, high caste and low, pure and impure. Kabir answered with a verse the Gurus placed in the Granth.
screen: `ONE CANDLE LIGHTS A HUNDRED.` → `WHICH FLAME IS HIGHER?` → `A CITY FULL OF LABELS.`

segments.voice: On Ang 1349, in Rag Prabhati, Kabir sings: awal allah noor upaaiaa kudrat ke sabh bande; ek noor te sabh jag upjiaa kaun bhale ko mande. First, God created the light; all people are creatures of that creation. From one light the whole world welled up; so who is good, and who is bad? Look at his words. Allah, the Arabic name for God. Noor, the Arabic and Persian word for light. Kudrat, creation, nature. A Muslim-born weaver, singing in words his Muslim neighbors would know, to a city full of Hindus too, and telling both the same thing: you came from the same light. The next lines, in paraphrase: people, don't wander in doubt. The Creator is in the creation, and the creation is in the Creator, filling every place. Six days ago, Guru Nanak said it with jot, light; Kabir says it with noor. He isn't saying everyone's the same, or that differences don't exist. He's saying the labels were never the source. Before the temple and the mosque, before castes and clans, there was one light, and everyone is lit from it. And the closing question is real: who is good, who is bad? Not a shrug about right and wrong, but a warning about sorting people by birth. That's why the verse sits so comfortably in the Gurus' book, beside their own songs of the same light.

segments.voice: Picture a stranger you passed recently, on the train, in a store, on a screen, and see in them a small flame lit from the same first light as yours; not a sentiment, just see it. Try it with one more stranger, then one more, as the breath slows. If it helps, say it quietly on the out-breath: from one light.
Kabir. Here, his verse in Prabhati: from one light the whole world came, so who is good and who is bad?
Your line: from one light. The flame came first; every label came later. Until tomorrow.

255.title: Kabir: the true warrior
255.hook: the brave one is the one who fights for the helpless and does not leave the field (Maru, Kabir, ang 1105)
255.howItsDone: Kabir's couplet on the true hero is often recited and sung by Sikhs, and it's commonly linked with the Sikh ideal of the saint-soldier who protects the defenseless.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir's verse of one light: from one light. Today, the gentle weaver says something surprisingly fierce.

A school hallway. A bigger kid has cornered a smaller one, and a small crowd watches, phones out, nobody moving. Then one kid, not the biggest, not the toughest, steps between them and says: that's enough. Everyone in that hallway knows, instantly, who the brave one was. Not the loudest. The one who stood up for someone who couldn't. Kabir, the weaver who sang of one light, has a couplet about exactly that kind of courage. Sikhs have loved it for centuries.
screen: `A CROWD, PHONES OUT.` → `ONE KID STEPS IN.` → `EVERYONE KNOWS WHO WAS BRAVE.`

segments.voice: On Ang 1105, among Kabir's saloks in Rag Maru, come two short couplets. The first sets the scene: the war drum sounds in the sky, the battle line is drawn, now is the time to fight. The second gives the definition: sooraa so pahichaaneeai ju larai deen ke het; purjaa purjaa kat marai kabahoo na chhaadai khet. Know that one as a hero who fights for the sake of the deen; who may be cut to pieces, but never leaves the field. Slow down on deen. In Punjabi it can mean the poor, the humble, the helpless. It's also close to an Arabic word, din, meaning faith. Commentators read it both ways, and both have been loved: the hero fights for the helpless, and for what is right. What the verse doesn't praise is just as clear: not the one who fights for loot or fame or land, not the one who wins. The one who stands for those who can't, and doesn't run. Why would a peaceful weaver sing this? Many Sikhs read the field two ways. The outer field: standing up for the weak, as later Sikhs, soldier-saints, would do. And the inner field, where the enemies are the five thieves, lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride, and staying on the field means not giving up on yourself. Either way, courage here isn't about strength. It's about who you're standing for, and whether you stay.

segments.voice: Think of one small thing that needs someone to stand up for it: a coworker talked over in meetings, a friend mocked in a group chat, a neighbor who can't carry their groceries, a quiet wrong you've been walking past. 256.title: Kabir: the death that delights
256.hook: the death the world fears fills Kabir with joy, for it brings the Beloved near (Kabir salok, ang 1365)
256.howItsDone: Kabir's saloks are read in the Guru Granth Sahib and quoted in Sikh reflections on death, where Sikh teaching discourages loud mourning and speaks of death as the soul's return.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir's true warrior: fight for the helpless. Today, Kabir looks at the thing the world fears, and smiles.

There's a whole vocabulary for not saying it: passed away, lost, gone. The subject gets changed. Nobody puts it on the calendar. That's human; it's a frightening thing. Then there's an old weaver who, when the subject comes up, doesn't flinch. He leans in. He says the thing the world is afraid of makes his heart glad. Not because he's tired of life. Because of who he thinks is waiting.
screen: `THE SUBJECT GETS CHANGED.` → `ONE WEAVER LEANS IN.` → `HIS HEART IS GLAD.`

segments.voice: Among Kabir's saloks near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, on Ang 1365: kabeer jis marne te jag darai mere man aanand; marne hee te paaeeai pooran parmaanand. Kabir, the death the world is so afraid of fills my mind with bliss; for it's through dying that one finds perfect, supreme joy. Aanand is joy, the same word as the Anand Sahib; parmaanand is supreme joy. Why joy? Remember the bride from day two hundred forty-four, waiting for her beloved, and Sohila's wedding date, already written. Kabir stands in that same picture. If the soul is a bride longing for God, the day of meeting isn't a disaster. It's the day she's been waiting for. There's a second layer. Kabir, and the Gurus after him, often speak of dying while alive: letting the ego die, the proud little I called haumai. In another salok, in paraphrase, Kabir says the whole world keeps dying, yet nobody knows how to die; die the kind of death after which you never die again. Some readers hear in it the death of ego, which frees a person to live without fear. Tradition adds a story people tell. A popular belief held that dying in Kashi, Benares, brought liberation, and dying in the town of Maghar did not. Kabir, it's said, went to Maghar to die, to show that it's the heart, not the place. In one hymn he says himself that at the end he left for Maghar; in another, that Kashi and Maghar are the same to one who has God in the heart.

257.title: Kabir's saloks
257.hook: near the Granth's end come over two hundred short couplets of Kabir, sharp and funny (ang 1364–1377)
257.howItsDone: Kabir's saloks are read near the end of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and some are quoted like proverbs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir on the death the world fears: what they fear, I welcome. Today, Kabir at his shortest and sharpest.

A proverb a grandmother said once that nobody in the family forgot. A line on a sticky note on the fridge. Two sentences someone posts that get screenshotted and passed around. Short things stick, because they can be carried. Near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib there's a whole run of Kabir's short sayings, two lines each, a couple of hundred of them, some tender, some sharp enough to sting, some genuinely funny. Today's word is what they're called: salok.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER'S PROVERB.` → `A NOTE ON THE FRIDGE.` → `SHORT THINGS STICK.`

segments.voice: A salok is a short verse, usually a couplet; the word comes from the Sanskrit shloka. Kabir's saloks fill the pages from Ang 1364 to 1377, more than two hundred of them. A few, marked with the Gurus' names, are replies or comments by Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan, tucked in among his. Each usually opens with his own name, Kabir, like a signature on a postcard. Here are three, in paraphrase. The very first: Kabir, my rosary is my tongue, and on it is God's Name. No beads needed; the prayer is in how you speak. Another: Kabir, I'm the worst of all; everyone else is good. Whoever understands it this way is my friend. A joke with a point: the quickest way to stop judging people is to start with yourself. And another: a true saint doesn't give up goodness even among a crowd of bad people, just as the sandalwood tree, wrapped in snakes, never stops being cool and fragrant. Notice the pattern. Each takes one ordinary picture, a rosary, a judge, a tree, and flips it. They're built to be memorized, quoted at the right moment, to sting a little and then stay with you. Some people keep a handful by heart, the way others keep proverbs. You don't have to read all two hundred. Three, carried well, will do.

258.title: Farid of Pakpattan
258.hook: Sheikh Farid, a Sufi of the Punjab centuries before Nanak, whose Punjabi verses the Gurus treasured
258.howItsDone: Farid's saloks and hymns are sung in Sikh kirtan and read in the Guru Granth Sahib; his shrine at Pakpattan, in Pakistan's Punjab, is visited by people of many faiths.

segments.voice: Yesterday, salok: sharp and short. Today, a new voice, older than Kabir, older than the Gurus, and often called the first poet of the Punjabi language.

A shrine stands in a small town in what is now Pakistan, and visitors of more than one faith come to it. The man remembered there was a Muslim holy man, a Sufi of the Punjab, who lived centuries before Guru Nanak. He wrote in the Punjabi of the villages, the language of the Guru Granth Sahib's heartland. And the Gurus kept his verses in their own book. Today, Farid of Pakpattan.
screen: `A SHRINE IN PAKPATTAN.` → `A SUFI, CENTURIES BEFORE NANAK.` → `KEPT IN THE GURUS' BOOK.`

segments.voice: Sheikh Farid, often called Baba Farid, was a Sufi, a Muslim mystic, of the Chishti order. He settled in a river town called Ajodhan, later renamed Pakpattan, and tradition says he taught, fasted, prayed and fed whoever came there. People called him Ganjshakar, treasury of sugar; there are many stories about why, and nobody can say which is true. What matters here is his language. Learned writing of his day was in Persian or Arabic. Farid's couplets are in the villagers' own Punjabi, and tradition counts them among the earliest poetry in the language. Hence the first Punjabi voice. The Guru Granth Sahib holds four of his hymns and more than a hundred saloks under his name. Sikh tradition says Guru Nanak met one of Farid's successors at Pakpattan and brought his verses home. Scholars debate whether every salok is by Farid himself or partly by later Sheikhs of his line who used his name. Either way, the Gurus heard their own teaching in them. Here's one, in paraphrase: don't speak even one harsh word, for the True Lord lives in everyone. Don't break anyone's heart; every heart is a priceless jewel. A Muslim saint in a Sikh book, speaking the people's language about the jewel in every heart: truth having many singers, again.

259.title: Farid: don't strike back
259.hook: if someone hits you, don't hit back; kiss their feet and go home (Farid salok, ang 1378)
259.howItsDone: Farid's saloks are read in the Guru Granth Sahib and quoted by Sikhs about humility and forgiveness in personal quarrels, alongside the Sikh duty to defend others who are wronged.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Farid of Pakpattan, the Sufi whose verses the Gurus kept: the first Punjabi voice. Today, a hard saying of his, and the end of a week.

A driver cuts across the lane, then leans on the horn as if it were the other person's fault. A relative makes the comment, the one that always comes, in front of everyone. The comeback is ready: the return honk, the line that'll put them in their place. It lands for a moment. Then it gets carried home and chewed on all night. Sheikh Farid has a couplet for exactly this moment.
screen: `THE HORN, THE COMMENT.` → `THE COMEBACK IS READY.` → `A MOMENT, THEN ALL NIGHT.`

segments.voice: On Ang 1378, among Farid's saloks: fareedaa jo tai maaran mukeeaan tinhaa na maare ghumm; aapnarai ghar jaaeeai pair tinhaa de chumm. Farid, those who strike you with their fists, don't turn around and strike them back. Kiss their feet, and go home. Kiss their feet? In the Punjab, touching someone's feet is a sign of respect and humility. He's asking for the opposite of revenge: meet the blow with humility, then walk away to your own home, your own peace, without carrying the fight with you. Farid isn't saying the blow was fine, or that wrong doesn't matter. Just before it, he tells the clever to bow their heads and look into their own collar. Later he says: do good to the one who does you wrong, and don't let anger into the mind. And notice the last line: go home. Don't stand there and take more. Don't keep the quarrel alive. Four days ago, Kabir praised the hero who fights for the helpless. So which is it? One reading holds the two together. When the blow is against you, your own pride, your own honor, you can let it go and go home. When the helpless are being crushed, you stand on the field. The ego doesn't get to fight for itself; the weak get defended. That's the whole week, in a way: a weaver at his loom, one light in everyone, a warrior for the helpless, a death that delights, Kabir's short sharp saloks, and Farid, the first Punjabi voice, saying go home in peace.
